summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived excerpt on Athanasius of Alexandria, covering his uncertain birth year, his early role against Arianism at the First Council of Nicaea, and his repeated conflicts with Arians and successive Roman emperors. It describes his succession as archbishop of Alexandria, his exile and return in 345 under Constans, and the renewed deposition after Constans's death in 350. The text stresses his persistence in defending Nicene orthodoxy despite exile and political opposition.
one_line: Biography of Athanasius of Alexandria, the 4th-century bishop who opposed Arianism and was repeatedly exiled by Roman emperors.
key_facts: Cornelius Clifford places Athanasius's birth no earlier than 296 and no later than 298.
The Orthodox Church places Athanasius's year of birth around 297.
The Arians accused Athanasius of not having attained the canonical age of 30 when he was ordained Patriarch of Alexandria in 328.
In 325, at the age of 27, Athanasius began his leading role against the Arians as his bishop's assistant during the First Council of Nicaea.
Roman emperor Constantine the Great convened the First Council of Nicaea in May–August 325.
The council addressed the Arian position that the Son of God, Jesus of Nazareth, is of a distinct substance from the Father.
Three years after the Council of Nicaea, Athanasius succeeded his mentor as archbishop of Alexandria.
Athanasius was known as "Athanasius Contra Mundum" (Latin for Athanasius Against the World).
Julian ordered Ecdicius, the Prefect of Egypt, to expel Athanasius on the ground that he had never been included in the imperial act of clemency.
Pythicodorus Trico communicated the edict of expulsion to the bishop and behaved with brutal insolence, according to the text.
On 23 October the people of Alexandria gathered to protest the emperor's decree, and Athanasius urged them to submit.
After the death of the replacement bishop Gregory in 345, Constans allowed Athanasius to return to Alexandria in October 345 amid enthusiastic demonstrations.
The return to Alexandria began a "golden decade" of peace and prosperity, during which Athanasius assembled documents for the Apology Against the Arians.
After Constans died in 350, pro-Arian Constantius became sole emperor.
An Alexandria local council in 350 replaced (or reaffirmed) Athanasius in his see.
